strengths: Novel theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 rigorously establishes DDPO-DSM equivalence, providing fundamental insight into what DDPO optimizes
Rigorous variance analysis: Theorem 2 formally quantifies variance increase from noisy conditioning with explicit κ(s,t) formula; proofs are sound and well-structured
Strong empirical validation of theory: Controlled CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 experiments (Figure 3) directly demonstrate that noisy-DSM converges slower, validating Theorem 2
Substantial practical speedups: Consistent 8-24× improvements across multiple metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore) and models (SD3.5M, FLUX) without quality degradation
Conceptual unification: Elegantly aligns diffusion RL with LLM RL—both optimize same objective with reward-dependent weighting, removing step-wise likelihood dependency
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with effective schematic figures, consistent notation, detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and clear mathematical exposition
Comprehensive empirical analysis: Ablations on timestep sampling, KL strength, and on-policy vs. off-policy; qualitative examples showing improvements
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: Only compared to Flow-GRPO; missing comparisons to original DDPO, DanceGRPO, TempFlow, and other reward-weighted approaches reduces confidence in claimed superiority

Ad-hoc design choice: Using w(t)=1 instead of standard ELBO weighting w(t) is justified only empirically, with vague explanation about 'visual quality vs. likelihood'; disconnects from the ELBO-based theoretical framework

Unquantified discretization error: Theorem 1 holds 'up to discretization error' but paper doesn't analyze magnitude. Flow-GRPO baseline uses plain Euler-Maruyama (which increases variance per footnote 2), leaving gap between theory and practice

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported despite G=24 batch size. Variance of key metrics (convergence time, GenEval scores) should be quantified to assess stability of 8-24× speedup claims

No variance measurements on main tasks: While Theorem 2 is rigorously proven, direct empirical measurement of AWM's variance reduction on RL tasks is absent. Figure 3 validates on pretraining but not on actual reward optimization
Limited scope of validation: No video generation experiments despite mentioning its importance; unclear if method generalizes beyond image generation to other domains

Incomplete reproducibility: Code link missing in abstract; reward function implementations (GenEval, OCR) not described; exact sampling/evaluation procedures and computational requirements not specified

Single benefit dimension: GenEval shows identical quality (0.95 vs 0.95); improvements on OCR/PickScore also show same performance with just faster convergence. Discussion of whether quality improvements are achievable would strengthen motivation

Underexplored design flexibility: While claiming AWM 'supports any sampler/noise level,' only Euler-Maruyama tested. Advanced ODE solvers and different noise schedules not evaluated despite being presented as advantages

Speedup attribution unclear: No decomposition of 8-24× speedup into components (variance reduction vs. training timestep reduction vs. other factors), making it difficult to attribute improvements to specific mechanisms

strengths: Novel theoretical insight establishing that DDPO implicitly performs DSM with noisy targets, providing new understanding of the objective mismatch between pretraining and RL post-training
Rigorous mathematical analysis with formal variance characterization (Theorem 2.3) showing κ(s,t) additional conditional covariance, supported by detailed proofs
Empirical validation of theoretical predictions through pretraining experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64 (Figure 3, Table 6) directly confirming variance predictions
Substantial practical speedups demonstrated consistently across multiple models (SD3.5M, FLUX) and metrics (GenEval 16.54×, OCR 19.13×, PickScore 34.67×) without quality degradation
Simple and generalizable method decoupled from sampler choice, enabling use with any ODE/SDE solver while maintaining alignment with pretraining objective
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including detailed ablation studies (Figures 7-8), multiple benchmarks, and reproducibility details (Algorithm 1, detailed hyperparameters in appendix)
Clear presentation with effective figures and mathematical exposition; code availability promised
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis operates at oracle level assuming population-level objectives and omitting Euler-Maruyama discretization error, which the paper acknowledges is 'inherent to DDPO formulation', creating gap between theory and practical discretized algorithms

Limited baseline comparisons—only evaluated against Flow-GRPO and TempFlow-GRPO, missing comparisons to DanceGRPO, other recent GRPO variants, and continuous-time RL approaches mentioned in related work
Lack of statistical significance testing with no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; unclear whether improvements like PickScore (23.01→23.11) are statistically significant

Speedup attribution unclear due to multiple confounding factors: different samplers (SA-Solver vs. unspecified baseline), different hyperparameters (w(t), timesteps, guidance scale, β, reference model), and different experimental configurations between early and later experiments

Extended training required for best quality: Table 2 shows AWM† needs 58 GPU hours for OCR 0.96 (vs. 21.76 hours for 0.92), somewhat undermining the '16.54× speedup' claim when comparing to best achievable quality

Missing critical ablations: no ablation of advantage weighting alone, no comparison of standard DSM with advantage weighting, no systematic study of w(t) impact despite switching between configurations

Variance analysis conditional on fixed xt; formal connection between reduced conditional variance and improved full optimization trajectory not established, relying on empirical validation rather than theoretical convergence guarantees
